questions.question: An administrator must ensure that users without the itil role cannot read Priority 1 Incident records, whether they open a list, a form, or call a web service API. What should be configured?

options.text: A UI policy on the Incident form
A role on the Incidents application module
A read ACL on the Incident table
A data policy on the Incident table

explanation.correct: Access control lists restrict access to data by requiring users to pass a set of requirements before they can interact with it. A read ACL on the incident table can require a role and use the Applies To filter to target only Priority 1 records. Failing a read ACL hides the records in lists and forms and also blocks retrieval through web service APIs. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI policies only apply to data entered on a form through the standard browser, so they cannot stop users from reading records in lists or through web service APIs.
Applications and modules list the roles required to view them, so a module role only controls who sees the module. Record and field access is secured by ACL rules, not by roles on modules.
Data policies enforce data consistency by setting mandatory and read-only states for fields. They do not decide which users may read a record.

source.excerpt: Most security settings are implemented using access controls. In addition to restricting CRUD operations, access control rules can restrict ServiceNow specific operations on tables and fields.

questions.question: An administrator can open and debug ACL records but cannot create a new ACL or save changes to an existing one. Which role must they elevate to in their session?

options.text: user_admin
security_admin
impersonator
role_delegator

explanation.correct: Normal admin users can view and debug access control rules, but creating or updating ACLs requires elevating privileges to the security_admin role. In the base system security_admin is the only elevated privilege role, and it lasts only for the current session, which is why the admin must elevate before editing. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: user_admin is a user administration role; the docs note it cannot even grant the admin role. Creating or changing ACLs specifically requires the elevated security_admin role.
The impersonator role is what lets a user impersonate other users. It does not grant the right to create or update access control rules.
role_delegator lets a user assign the roles they hold to members of a group. It has nothing to do with editing ACL records, which requires security_admin.

source.excerpt: In the base system, only the default system administrator has the security admin role. Others with the admin role must also be granted the security admin role to manage ACLs.

questions.question: An administrator elevated to security_admin yesterday to update ACLs, then logged out at the end of the day. After logging back in today, what is the status of that elevated role?

options.text: It stays active until deselected in the Elevate Roles dialog
It ended with the session, so the admin must elevate again
It is now saved as a permanent role on the admin's user record
It returns automatically because the admin role contains it

explanation.correct: An elevated privilege role lasts only for the duration of the user session; a session timeout or logout removes it. Users do not have elevated roles on login and must manually elevate again. Because the admin logged out yesterday, the security_admin elevation ended and must be re-selected through Elevate Roles before editing ACLs. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/c_ElevatedPrivilege.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Deselecting in the dialog is one way to end elevation, but logout also terminates elevated privileges with the session, so nothing is still active today.
Elevation never becomes a permanent assignment. By default users do not have elevated privilege roles upon login and must manually elevate each session.
The Security Administrator role is not inherited by the admin role, and an elevated role must be manually elevated even when another role contains it.

source.excerpt: Elevated roles allow modification of the access control list. These roles last only for your session. They end with logout, session time out, or user impersonation.

questions.question: A security administrator adds a Deny-Unless read ACL to a custom table that already has an Allow-If read ACL. When a user requests a record from that table, how are the two decision types evaluated?

options.text: Allow-If first; a passing Allow-If ACL skips the Deny-Unless
The ACL that was created most recently is evaluated first
Deny-Unless first; if it fails, access is denied outright
Deny-Unless first; if it passes, access is granted outright

explanation.correct: Deny-Unless ACLs take priority over Allow-If ACLs because they are evaluated first. A Deny-Unless ACL denies access unless its roles, conditions, security attributes and script are met; if it fails, access is denied. If it passes, evaluation continues, and because an Allow-If ACL also matches, that Allow-If ACL must still permit access. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/acl-denial-behavior.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The order is the reverse: Deny-Unless ACLs are evaluated first and take priority, so a passing Allow-If ACL cannot bypass a failing Deny-Unless ACL.
Evaluation priority comes from the decision type, not from when the ACL was created. Deny-Unless ACLs are evaluated before Allow-If ACLs.
A passing Deny-Unless ACL only lets evaluation proceed. When an Allow-If ACL also matches, access is granted only if that Allow-If ACL explicitly permits it.

source.excerpt: The system checks deny rules first. If any deny rules conditions are unmet, access is blocked, requiring all matching deny rule conditions to be satisfied for access to proceed.

questions.question: An administrator is creating a custom table in System Definition > Tables and wants basic security rules generated for it, along with a role that users need to access the table. What should they do on the table form?

options.text: Select the Extensible check box in the Controls section
Select Create access controls and enter a User role
Set Accessible from to This application scope only
Clear Allow access to this table via web services

explanation.correct: On the table form, the Create access controls check box creates basic security rules for the new table. Once it is selected, the User role field becomes available so the administrator can enter a new role name or pick an existing role that is required to access the table. This produces the ACLs and role in one step. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/t_CreateATable.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Extensible only controls whether other tables are allowed to extend this table. It does not create any security rules or access roles.
Accessible from defines which application scopes can access the table. It is an application access setting and does not generate ACLs for users.
Clearing this check box prevents inbound web service queries to the table. It does not create the basic security rules or a required role.

source.excerpt: With system created access controls, it is rare to have a table with no access control rules. When a table is created, access controls are automatically created.

questions.question: A user passes a table-level ACL but fails a field-level ACL. What access does the user have?

options.text: Full access to the record including all fields
No access to the record at all
Access to the record but not to that specific field
Read-only access to all fields

explanation.correct: Access controls are checked in order, starting with table access and then field access. Failing a table rule denies access to all. Passing a table rule but failing a field rule denies access to that field only. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The user would be denied access to the specific field that failed the ACL check.
Table-level access was granted, so the user can see the record, just not the restricted field.
The field restriction is specific to the failed ACL, not a global read-only state.

source.excerpt: Access controls are checked in order, starting with table access and then field access. Failing a table rule denies access to all passing a table rule, but failing a field rule denies access to that field.

questions.question: What does an upward arrow next to a user's avatar indicate in ServiceNow?

options.text: The user has unread notifications
The user has activated elevated privileges
The user is impersonating another user
The user has pending approvals

explanation.correct: An upward arrow next to your avatar indicates activated elevated privileges. This visual indicator helps administrators know when they have temporary elevated security access. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Unread notifications are indicated differently, typically with a badge number.
Impersonation is indicated by a different visual cue showing the impersonated user.
Pending approvals appear in the approval modules, not as avatar indicators.

source.excerpt: An upward arrow next to your avatar indicates activated elevated privileges.

questions.question: How do ACL rules for parent tables apply to child tables?

options.text: They don't apply - each table needs its own ACLs
ACL rules for parent tables apply to their child tables
Child tables override all parent table ACLs
Only admin-created ACLs are inherited

explanation.correct: ACL rules for parent tables apply to their child tables. This inheritance model means security settings on a parent table like 'task' automatically apply to child tables like 'incident' and 'change_request'. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: ACLs are inherited from parent to child tables in ServiceNow's table hierarchy.
Child tables don't automatically override parent ACLs; they inherit and can have additional ACLs.
All ACLs on parent tables are inherited, regardless of who created them.

source.excerpt: ACL rules for parent tables apply to their child tables.

questions.question: What are the three main security modules typically used by system administrators?

options.text: Users, Groups, and Roles
Security, ACL list, and High Security Settings
Authentication, Authorization, and Audit
Login, Password, and Session

explanation.correct: System administrators typically use three security modules: Security, ACL list, and High Security Settings. These modules provide the tools needed to manage access controls and security configurations. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: While Users, Groups, and Roles are important, they are not the three main security modules.
These are security concepts, not the specific module names in ServiceNow.
These relate to authentication features, not the main security administration modules.

source.excerpt: System administrators typically use three security modules-- security, ACL list, and high security settings.

questions.question: What limitation applies to users with the admin role when impersonating another user?

options.text: They cannot impersonate any users
They can only impersonate users in their group
They cannot impersonate the security_admin role or elevate privileges during impersonation
They must have manager approval to impersonate

explanation.correct: Admins cannot impersonate the security admin role or elevate privileges during impersonation to access high security functions. This is a security measure to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive security configurations. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Admins can impersonate other users, but with certain restrictions.
Impersonation is not limited to group membership for admins.
Manager approval is not required for admin impersonation by default.

source.excerpt: However, admins cannot impersonate the security admin role or elevate privileges during impersonation to access high security functions.

questions.question: Which components does ServiceNow use to ensure security for CRUD operations? (Choose two)

options.text: User authentication/login managed via users, groups, and roles
Automatic data encryption at rest
Application and module access controlled by roles
Mandatory two-factor authentication

explanation.correct: ServiceNow ensures security for CRUD operations with: user authentication/login managed via users, groups and roles; application and module access controlled by roles; and database access managed by system properties and table/field access controls. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: While encryption may be available, it's not one of the core CRUD security mechanisms described.
MFA is an optional security feature, not a core CRUD operation security mechanism.

source.excerpt: ServiceNow ensures security for CRUD operations with, user authentication/login, managed via users, groups and roles, application and module access controlled by roles.

questions.question: What is the purpose of user impersonation in ServiceNow?

options.text: To permanently change a user's password
To test the platform from another user's perspective and troubleshoot access issues
To delete another user's account
To merge two user accounts together

explanation.correct: Impersonation allows administrators to test the platform from another user's perspective. This is useful for troubleshooting access issues, verifying that security configurations work correctly, and understanding what a specific user can see and do.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Password changes are managed through user administration, not impersonation.
Account deletion is a separate administrative function, not related to impersonation.
Account merging is not a feature of impersonation.

source.excerpt: Impersonation allows administrators to test and troubleshoot by viewing the platform as another user would see it.

questions.question: What must a user have to access data in ServiceNow?

options.text: Only a role
Only ACL access
Both a role AND ACL access
Group membership only

explanation.correct: A user needs BOTH a role AND ACL access to see data. Roles grant access to application modules, while ACLs control record-level access. Both must be satisfied for a user to access specific data.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Roles alone grant module access but don't control data access without ACLs.
ACLs control data access but users also need appropriate roles to access modules.
Group membership helps organize users but doesn't directly grant data access without roles and ACLs.

source.excerpt: A user needs BOTH a role AND ACL access to see data. Roles grant access to application modules, while ACLs control record-level access.

questions.question: A system administrator needs to grant a user temporary elevated access to modify ACLs. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Permanently assign the security_admin role to the user
Have the user activate elevated privileges for their session
Give the user the admin role
Disable all ACLs temporarily

explanation.correct: Elevated privileges allow temporary access to higher security functions and last only for the current session. This is more secure than permanently assigning roles because access automatically ends with logout, timeout, or impersonation. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Permanently assigning security_admin violates the principle of least privilege for temporary needs.
Admin role alone doesn't grant ACL modification - security_admin is still required.
Disabling ACLs would create significant security risks and is not recommended.

source.excerpt: Elevated roles allow modification of the access control list. These roles last only for your session.

questions.question: Which statements about the admin role in ServiceNow are true? (Choose two)

options.text: Admins have access to all platform features and can override access controls
Admins can automatically modify ACLs without any additional roles
The admin role should be assigned cautiously
Admins can impersonate security_admin during impersonation sessions

explanation.correct: Admins have access to all platform features and can override access controls, so the role should be assigned cautiously. However, admins cannot modify ACLs without security_admin and cannot impersonate security_admin during impersonation. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Admins need the security_admin role in addition to admin to modify ACLs.
Admins cannot impersonate security_admin or elevate privileges during impersonation.

source.excerpt: Admins have access to all platform features and can override access controls so assign this role cautiously.

questions.question: What is the recommended method for assigning roles to users in ServiceNow?

options.text: Assign roles directly to individual user records
Add users to groups and assign roles to the groups
Use update sets to assign roles
Configure roles through the CMDB

explanation.correct: Rather than adding roles to individual users, the recommended approach is to add the user to a group and assign the role to the group. This makes maintenance easier when people transfer to different roles in the organization.

wrongAnswers.explanation: While possible, assigning roles directly to users makes maintenance difficult when organizational changes occur.
Update sets are for migrating configuration changes between instances, not for role assignment.
The CMDB tracks configuration items, not user roles.

questions.question: What indicates that elevated privileges are activated for an administrator's session?

options.text: A lock icon appears in the navigation menu
An upward arrow appears next to the user's avatar
The background color of the instance changes
A notification email is sent to the security team

explanation.correct: An upward arrow next to your avatar indicates activated elevated privileges. These roles last only for your session and end with logout, session timeout, or user impersonation.

wrongAnswers.explanation: There is no lock icon for elevated privileges; the indicator is an upward arrow by the avatar.
The background color does not change for elevated privileges.
No email notification is sent when elevating privileges.

questions.question: Which actions can users WITHOUT any assigned roles perform in ServiceNow? (Choose 2)

options.text: View a dashboard
Create business rules
Access the service catalog
Manage access control lists

explanation.correct: Users without any assigned roles can still log in and access common actions such as viewing a dashboard, accessing the service catalog, viewing knowledge articles, and taking surveys. These are often referred to as self-service users.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Creating business rules requires administrative roles.
Managing ACLs requires the security_admin role.

questions.question: Which statement about user impersonation is TRUE?

options.text: Any user can impersonate another user
Impersonation allows access to security incidents even if you don't have those roles
Only users with the admin or impersonator role can impersonate other users
Impersonation persists across multiple login sessions

explanation.correct: Only admins and users with the impersonator role can impersonate other users to test their access. When impersonating a user with a specific admin role, you cannot access certain features like security incidents unless you already have those roles.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Only users with the admin or impersonator role can impersonate others.
When impersonating, you cannot access features like security incidents unless you already have those specific roles.
Impersonation does not persist across login sessions.

questions.question: A user has the catalog_admin role. What access does this provide?

options.text: Only access to the Service Catalog application
Only access to user criteria modules
Access to all Service Catalog and user criteria modules, plus additional catalog_admin permissions
Full admin access to all platform features

explanation.correct: The catalog_admin role includes permissions from both user_criteria_admin and catalog roles, providing access to all applications and modules of both roles plus any permissions specific to catalog_admin.

wrongAnswers.explanation: catalog_admin includes more than just the catalog role — it also contains user_criteria_admin permissions.
catalog_admin includes user criteria access but also catalog and additional permissions.
catalog_admin provides access to catalog-related features, not full admin access.

questions.question: A security administrator wants one place to view the instance's hardening compliance score, the top non-compliant hardening settings, and the results of security scans. Which application should they use?

options.text: Contextual Security Manager
ServiceNow Security Center
Instance Security Center
High Security Settings

explanation.correct: Security Center is a free application, installed by default since the Vancouver release, that helps organizations maintain the security of their ServiceNow deployments. Its security configuration console shows the hardening compliance score, trends, the top non-compliant hardening settings and security scan results, which matches every need in this scenario. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/security-center/sec-center-v2.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Contextual Security Manager controls read, write, create and delete authorization through ACL rules. It does not provide compliance scores or scan results.
Instance Security Center reached end of sales in September 2024 and is no longer supported or available for activation; Security Center replaces it.
High Security Settings is a set of security properties and features such as the security_admin role and default deny, not a dashboard of compliance and scan results.

questions.question: An administrator needs to prevent users in the 'itil' group from editing the Priority field on Incident records, but they should still be able to view it. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Create a write ACL on the incident.priority field that excludes the itil role
Remove the Priority field from the incident form
Create a UI Policy that makes Priority read-only for itil users
Delete the Priority field from the Incident table

explanation.correct: A UI Policy with a condition checking the user's role can make the Priority field read-only for itil users while keeping it visible. This is the standard approach for role-based field-level restrictions on forms.

wrongAnswers.explanation: While ACLs can control write access, a field-level write ACL that excludes itil would also affect other operations. UI Policy is more targeted for form-level display control.
Removing the field prevents viewing it entirely, which contradicts the requirement to keep it visible.
Deleting a core field like Priority would break system functionality and is never appropriate.

questions.question: Which three elements make up an Access Control List (ACL) rule in ServiceNow? (Choose 3)

options.text: The object being secured (table/field)
The operation (read, write, create, delete)
The permissions required (role, condition, script)
The time zone of the user
The browser type being used

explanation.correct: An ACL rule consists of three parts: the object (what is being protected — a table, field, or record), the operation (what action is being controlled — read, write, create, or delete), and the permissions (who is allowed — defined by roles, conditions, and/or scripts).

wrongAnswers.explanation: Time zone is a user preference setting, not a component of ACL rules.
Browser type is not relevant to ACL evaluation.

questions.question: A security administrator notices two Allow-If read ACLs on the incident.number field at the same point in the processing order. A user passes one of them and fails the other. What happens?

options.text: The user can read the field, since passing one is enough
Access is denied because every matching ACL must be passed
Only the older ACL is evaluated and the newer one is ignored
The more restrictive ACL wins, so the field is hidden

explanation.correct: When two or more ACLs match at the same point in the processing order, the user only has to pass any one of them. The docs use this exact example: with two field ACLs on incident.number, a user who passes one rule can access the number field even if they fail the other. The all-must-pass rule applies only to multiple Deny-Unless ACLs. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Requiring every matching ACL to pass is the behavior for multiple Deny-Unless ACLs on a resource. For Allow-If ACLs at the same point, passing any one is enough.
Both ACLs are considered. If two or more ACLs match at the same point in the processing order, passing any one of them grants access.
There is no most-restrictive-wins rule for Allow-If ACLs at the same processing point; a user who passes one of them has access to the field.

questions.question: A new employee needs access to the Incident table but should NOT be able to delete any records. Which ACL configuration achieves this?

options.text: Grant read, write, and create ACLs but do not grant a delete ACL for the user's role
Create a delete ACL that explicitly denies the user's role
Remove the Incident module from the user's application menu
Set the 'active' field to read-only on the incident form

explanation.correct: In ServiceNow, if no ACL grants a specific operation for a role, that operation is denied by default. By granting read/write/create but not creating a delete ACL for the role, delete access is implicitly denied.

wrongAnswers.explanation: While explicit deny works, the simpler approach is to not grant delete access at all. ACLs deny by default when no matching rule grants access.
Removing a module from navigation doesn't prevent access to the table through direct URL, lists, or other means.
Making the active field read-only doesn't prevent record deletion.

questions.question: Which user property determines the language displayed in the ServiceNow interface?

options.text: The browser's Accept-Language header only
The Language field on the user's System Properties
The Preferred language field on the user record
The instance's system locale setting only

explanation.correct: The Preferred language field on the sys_user record determines the interface language for that user. If not set, the system falls back to the instance default language.

wrongAnswers.explanation: The browser language header may influence initial detection but the user record setting takes precedence.
System Properties control instance-wide settings, not individual user language preferences.
The system locale is the fallback, but individual user settings override it.

questions.question: A group manager is designated as a role delegator by an administrator and wants to update her team's access. Which action can she now perform?

options.text: Assign roles she holds to members of a group
Assign the admin role to any member of her group
Delegate her role_delegator role to another member
Grant any role in the instance to her group members

explanation.correct: Role delegators are users that administrators allow to assign roles within groups, but they can only assign roles that they already have. On the Delegate Roles in Group form, the roles available for delegating are only the roles the role_delegator has, and the docs note delegators can assign roles inherited from a group as well as roles an administrator assigned to them. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/c_DelegateRoles.html and https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/t_RoleDelegation.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: By default the admin role cannot be delegated, so a role delegator cannot hand it out even to members of a group she manages.
A user with the role_delegator role can't delegate that role to other group members; role_delegator is non-delegable by default.
Delegators are limited to roles they already hold; the Roles to delegate list only offers roles that the role_delegator has.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid method to assign a role to a user in ServiceNow?

options.text: Adding the role directly to the user's Roles related list
Adding the user to a group that has the role
Inheriting the role through the role hierarchy (contained roles)
Setting the role in the user's email signature

explanation.correct: Email signatures have no connection to role assignment in ServiceNow. Roles are assigned directly to users, through group membership, or through role inheritance (contained roles).

wrongAnswers.explanation: Direct role assignment via the Roles related list is a standard method.
Group-based role assignment is the recommended method for managing roles at scale.
Role inheritance through 'contains' relationships is a valid built-in mechanism.

questions.question: An administrator on a new instance confirms that the High Security Settings plugin is active and wants to know what it provides. Which capability is part of High Security Settings?

options.text: An elevated security_admin role for changing ACLs
Automatic encryption of the tables in the database
Multi-factor authentication enforced at user login
Blocking of inbound SOAP and CSV web service requests

explanation.correct: High Security Settings, active by default on new instances, provides a Security Administrator role, elevated privileges, a default deny property, property access controls and ACLs. The plugin separates user functionality from access control management by requiring administrators to explicitly elevate into security_admin before making access control changes. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/exploring-high-security-settings.html and https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/instance-security-hardening-settings/sc-high-security-plugin.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Database encryption is not among the High Security Settings features, which cover default properties, default deny, the security_admin role, elevated privileges and ACLs.
Multi-factor authentication is not one of the features delivered by High Security Settings; the plugin focuses on access control and hardened properties.
High Security Settings properties require authorization for inbound SOAP and CSV requests rather than blocking them outright.
